accepted.reason: Observation-target alignment is good: hospitalization rates plausibly track infections with a short lag, and surveillance notes explicitly endorse delayed_I. With 31 training weeks (single-season) and moderate peakiness, SEIRS without fractional memory is parsimonious enough while allowing waning if present. Delay=2 is a reasonable default and less likely than longer delays to mis-time the peak.

Also aligned with the recommended delayed_I mapping and avoids adding a weakly identifiable H compartment. However, delay=3 increases risk of peak misalignment and short-horizon forecast phase error if the true admissions lag is closer to 1–2 weeks or varies over time; still worth keeping as an alternative lag hypothesis.

SEIR + delayed_I is well-aligned and more parsimonious than SEIRS, which can be advantageous with only 31 weeks of training data. It provides a useful check against over-parameterization from waning immunity when the season does not clearly exhibit reinfection/waning effects.

rejected.reason: Although H maps directly to the hospitalization-rate target, an explicit H compartment is flagged as weakly identifiable for short single-season series. SEIHR adds extra transition rates (e.g., I→H, H→R) that can confound with transmission and recovery, risking unstable fits without clear additional signal in 31 weeks.

I+H is not well-aligned to an admissions-focused hospitalization-rate target and can blur interpretation/scale (mixing prevalence-like and admissions/severity-like components). It also inherits SEIHR identifiability risks while adding an additional observation mixture that can be hard to disentangle in short data.

suggested_edits.edit: Clarify that delay=3 is intended as a competing lag hypothesis to be compared qualitatively against delay=2 (phase alignment), and note that a fixed 3-week lag may be brittle if the admissions lag is shorter or time-varying within the season.

Add a note that SEIR is preferred when there is no clear late-season rebound/waning signature; if the tail shows sustained elevation or secondary rise, SEIRS may be necessary. Keep fractional memory off to avoid overfitting given n_train=31.

If retained for completeness, explicitly constrain/regularize hospitalization-process parameters conceptually (e.g., keep H duration simple) and emphasize heightened identifiability risk in single-season data; otherwise deprioritize in favor of delayed_I mappings.

If kept at all, justify I+H with a concrete surveillance interpretation (e.g., blended severe-case proxy) and warn that it may distort level/shape for an admissions-rate target; otherwise drop due to weak semantic alignment and added confounding.
